beats.narration_slice: It’s often called the lipstick effect.
beats.visual: Ink-wash editorial still of a single lipstick tube standing upright beside a nearly empty coin purse on warm ivory paper, the lipstick-red tip acting as the only vivid accent while muted charcoal shadows suggest financial strain.
beats.purpose: introduce the lipstick effect as the idea linking a small cosmetic purchase with economic pressure
beats.visual_fingerprint: single lipstick and open coin purse; static tabletop still life; close three-quarter view; warm ivory editorial surface; lipstick-red focal accent; centered asymmetrical composition
beats.continuity: Begins the body with the core symbolic pairing of lipstick and limited money, establishing the recurring editorial paper world.

beats.narration_slice: Tight budgets can push bigger luxuries aside.
beats.visual: Ink-wash scene of a hand sliding a large elegant shopping bag and a luxury shoe box away from the foreground while a thin wallet with only a few coins remains near the center, rendered in recession-gray taupe and charcoal.
beats.purpose: show expensive discretionary purchases being removed when money becomes scarce
beats.visual_fingerprint: hands pushing large luxury bag and shoe box away; medium overhead angle; household budgeting table zone; muted taupe objects; diagonal outward motion composition
beats.continuity: Moves from the small lipstick symbol to a wider budgeting action, showing what gets sacrificed before smaller comforts.

beats.narration_slice: Lipstick can still feel like affordable comfort.
beats.visual: Ink-wash close-up of an ordinary shopper's hand selecting one modest lipstick from a sparse cosmetic counter while larger luxury items blur into pale gray wash behind it; the small red cosmetic feels warm and attainable.
beats.purpose: show lipstick functioning as a comparatively affordable personal treat
beats.visual_fingerprint: hand choosing one lipstick at modest cosmetics counter; intimate close-up; eye-level retail angle; soft sage and ivory surroundings; small red object isolated against subdued background
beats.continuity: Contrasts the discarded large luxuries with one small purchase that remains within reach.

beats.narration_slice: Juliet Schor described this behavior in 1998.
beats.visual: Late-1990s editorial research scene in ink wash: a female sociologist figure at a wooden desk studying consumer notes and books beside a small lipstick, with period-appropriate clothing, paper files, and an older desktop computer shape kept free of readable text.
beats.purpose: attribute an early description of this consumer behavior to Juliet Schor in the late 1990s
beats.visual_fingerprint: female researcher at late-1990s desk; seated reading and annotating; medium side profile; academic office setting; bulky period computer and lipstick as symbolic objects; left-weighted composition
beats.continuity: Shifts from present-tense consumer behavior into its historical discussion, retaining the lipstick as a small visual bridge.

beats.narration_slice: Leonard Lauder popularized the lipstick index in 2001.
beats.visual: Early-2000s department-store cosmetics floor rendered in soft ink wash, with a suited male executive observing rows of lipstick displays from the aisle; period packaging silhouettes and restrained red accents evoke the era without any readable branding.
beats.purpose: show Leonard Lauder's early-2000s association with popularizing the lipstick index
beats.visual_fingerprint: suited executive observing cosmetic display; medium-wide rear three-quarter shot; early-2000s department-store aisle; repeated lipstick rows; perspective lines leading toward figure
beats.continuity: Advances chronologically from academic observation to the idea's public popularization in the cosmetics business.

beats.narration_slice: He suggested lipstick sales might rise when the economy weakens.
beats.visual: Editorial ink-wash metaphor showing a gray descending economic slope on one side while several lipstick tubes rise upward like simple physical markers on the other, with no numbers, labels, arrows, or chart text.
beats.purpose: visualize the proposed inverse relationship between a weakening economy and rising lipstick sales
beats.visual_fingerprint: descending gray economic slope opposed by ascending lipstick objects; symbolic action; wide graphic composition; abstract ivory paper field; charcoal downturn versus red upward accents; strong diagonal counter-motion
beats.continuity: Extracts Lauder's proposition from the retail setting and turns it into a simple visual relationship.

beats.narration_slice: The idea became a quirky recession signal.
beats.visual: Ink-wash metaphor of a lipstick tube perched like the needle of an old-fashioned economic gauge beside a small storm cloud over a miniature shopping street, playful but restrained and entirely free of labels or numbers.
beats.purpose: show how the lipstick idea came to be treated as an informal signal of recession
beats.visual_fingerprint: lipstick acting as gauge needle above miniature retail street; whimsical symbolic setup; slightly high angle; isolated editorial vignette; storm cloud and ochre gauge frame; circular composition
beats.continuity: Turns the proposed sales relationship into the quirky indicator metaphor that made the concept memorable.

beats.narration_slice: Later downturns did not repeat the pattern reliably.
beats.visual: Ink-wash tabletop with several recession-era shopping moments represented by scattered lipstick tubes pointing in inconsistent directions among faded receipts, coins, and closed wallets, creating an irregular pattern rather than a clean trend.
beats.purpose: show that subsequent economic downturns produced inconsistent lipstick-sales behavior
beats.visual_fingerprint: scattered lipsticks oriented unpredictably among wallets and receipts; top-down wide still life; household evidence table; alternating gray and faded red marks; deliberately irregular radial scatter
beats.continuity: Breaks the neat signal from the prior beat by replacing a single clear indicator with contradictory outcomes.

beats.narration_slice: So lipstick sales are not a dependable economic indicator.
beats.visual: Editorial ink-wash image of a lipstick balanced precariously on a tilted brass scale opposite a cluster of mixed economic objects such as groceries, fuel canister silhouette, coins, and a house key, emphasizing that one cosmetic cannot reliably represent the whole economy.
beats.purpose: make clear that lipstick sales should not be treated as a reliable economic measurement
beats.visual_fingerprint: lipstick on unstable balance scale versus mixed household-economic objects; medium frontal shot; neutral paper void; restrained brass ochre and charcoal; opposing weighted composition
beats.continuity: Converts the inconsistent evidence into the conclusion that lipstick alone cannot carry the weight of economic diagnosis.

beats.narration_slice: And “lipstick syndrome” is not a recognized medical diagnosis.
beats.visual: Ink-wash still of a lipstick resting outside a closed doctor's medical bag and stethoscope, clearly separated from the clinical objects by open ivory space; the cosmetic remains vivid red while the medical items stay subdued charcoal and taupe.
beats.purpose: distinguish the informal phrase lipstick syndrome from an actual medical diagnosis
beats.visual_fingerprint: lipstick physically separated from closed medical bag and stethoscope; static close-medium composition; clean ivory negative space; clinical objects muted charcoal; strong spatial separation between cosmetic and medicine
beats.continuity: Ends the body by separating the informal consumer-behavior label from clinical medicine, setting up the closing clarification.
